book_risk._note: Book-level risk (added 2026-07-19 after an audit found every binding constraint was arithmetic on ONE proposal while portfolio_beta / shared_left_tail / corr_to_book were computed by tools/correlation.py and consumed only as prose). Four controls, all in tools/book_risk.py, all pure. (1) max_factor_stack_pct: aggregate notional across factor_map.AI_STACK_DRIVERS. The 2% per-driver risk cap permits ~2 positions per driver, so 8 positions across 4 AI-stack drivers was 100% AI exposure passing every existing limit - a per-driver cap is not a factor cap. (2) gap_adjusted_heat: the 8% heat cap sums (cost-stop)*qty, which assumes stops FILL AT THE STOP - contradicted by execution_costs.stop_gap_atr_fraction (0.5) in this same file, and by the only closed stop in the ledger (DELL plan stop 408.00, fill 389.75, 4.5% through, realized -13.5% on a position sized for 1%). Heat now adds the modelled gap-through, using correlation only to decide how much of the book gaps on the same morning - NEVER to hand budget back, since the plain sum is already the fully-correlated case. Unknown correlation assumes the worst. (3) max_portfolio_beta: MV-weighted against EQUITY not invested capital, so a half-cash book reads as half-exposed. (4) stress_scenarios: named shocks priced against the book the proposal WOULD create; losses deliberately NOT floored at stops, because a shock worth naming is one where stops gap. driver_shocks key __ai_stack__ shocks the whole factor group. All four fail CLOSED on unverifiable inputs, matching the portfolio_heat_unverifiable precedent.

recent.topic: Stop distance vs. holding horizon: the √t noise band, and why entry location (not stop width) is the binding lever on multi-week swings
recent.summary: A stop has one job: fire on evidence the thesis broke, not on ordinary noise. Kaminski & Lo (SIFR RR 63, 2008; J. Financial Markets 18(C):234-254, 2014) prove that under a random walk, stop-loss rules ALWAYS decrease expected return; they only add value when returns exhibit momentum/positive serial correlation, generating what they call a 'stopping premium' proportional to return persistence (empirically 50-100bp/month during stop-out periods, US equities 1950-2004). So a stop placed inside the random-walk noise band is a pure expected-return tax. The quantitative half comes from volatility scaling: noise excursion grows with the SQUARE ROOT of time, so a stop sized off a one-day ATR is roughly √N too tight for an N-day hold (√45 ≈ 6.7). Danielsson & Zigrand (J. Banking & Finance 30(10):2701-2713, 2006) show the √t rule is only valid under iid normal returns and under jump diffusion 'leads to a systematic underestimation of risk, whereby the degree of underestimation worsens with the time horizon [and] the jump intensity' — so for equities with earnings inside the horizon, ATR×√N is a FLOOR on the noise band, not a ceiling. The decisive consequence: NO static entry stop inside a 15% cap can cover a 45-day noise band. This is not a reason to widen stops (the cap and the 2:1 RR floor forbid it) — it is the proof that stop width is not the free lever. Entry location is. The stop must only survive until the thesis STARTS working, which is why the Chandelier Exit (verified formula
recent.how_to_apply: Before any BUY, run the horizon-vs-noise test: compare my stop distance (%) against the name's daily ATR% × √(days until the nearest real catalyst) — NOT the full holding_horizon_days. If the stop is inside that band, the setup is asking a coin-flip to pay me: either move the entry down near the structural swing low so the same stop sits beyond the band, shorten the stated horizon to match what the stop can actually survive, or pass. Never widen the stop to fix this — the 15% cap and the 2:1 RR floor make wide stops fail geometry anyway, and stop_engineering's min_stop_distance_pct is a ONE-DAY floor that I must stop treating as horizon-adequate. closed_trades.thesis: Dell is the best risk/reward in an extended AI-server complex: it pairs elite momentum (+143% 3m, +202% 6m) with the cheapest valuation in the group (forward P/E ~20.9, P/S 2.2) and a constructive entry, having pulled back only 2.2% from its 20-day high while sitting 4.1% off its 52-week high near a buy point. The 29% collapse in Super Micro is a direct tailwind, consolidating enterprise/AI-server share toward Dell as customers de-risk suppliers. Q1 fundamentals (revenue $23.4B, net income $965M) confirm profitable scale, and the current tape ('Dell Stock Nears Buy Point') shows institutional demand building. With no earnings until 9/3, a 45-day swing captures the momentum leg without event risk.

HPE is the most valuation-protected way to own the AI-server/networking buildout in a tape where reaccelerating inflation (CPI 4.27%) and a rising 10-year (4.56%) are punishing rich multiples. It trades at just ~12.2x forward earnings and 1.67x sales - the cheapest in the server group - after a record fiscal Q2 and the completed Juniper acquisition, which adds a scaled networking franchise. Sell-side has responded with a +40.5% 30-day upward EPS revision, yet the stock is consolidating (1m +1.4%) and sits 23.8% below its 52-week high, so estimates are rising while price has not re-rated. The same SMCI collapse (-29%) that helps Dell consolidates enterprise AI-server demand toward HPE as customers de-risk suppliers. With the last print already behind it (38 days ago) and no earnings inside the 40-day window, this is a clean cheap-re-rating swing.

recent.note: Weekly self-review: Last Friday's stated change was to get the insider Form-4 feed pre-classified into sponsor/10b5-1 vs. discretionary officer transactions instead of handing me hundreds of noisy rows -- that fix landed and it worked: tonight's insider_activity block gave clean, directly actionable signals (BSX bullish_cluster_buying, 3 officers buying $554K with zero sells; ZS notable_discretionary_selling), a real improvement over last week's noise. The trading result this week was rougher: my only two closed trades, DELL and HPE, both lost (-$135 and -$45, 0% win rate, avg R -0.98), and with only 2 closed trades this is anecdote-level evidence per my own sample-size rules -- I am not inventing hard rules from it, but the pattern is worth naming honestly. Both losses shared the same demand_driver (hyperscaler_server_capex/servers_hardware) dressed up as two separate theses when the actual catalyst language ('SMCI collapse consolidates AI-server share') was nearly identical -- bad reasoning (thin diversification), not bad data, and it is exactly the clustering the system's theme-risk cap now exists to prevent. HPE's exit was graded process_fail: I closed it at $46.08 without its $43.75 stop being hit and without a clearly named invalidator firing -- conviction cracked, not thesis broken, which is the discretionary-exit mistake I need to stop making. What I got right: after those two losses on 7/15, the book stayed disciplined and all-cash through the rest of the week, including declining a real-looking AMD dip-buy today because my own stated trigger condition (post-event confirmation) was not actually met. A new engineering issue surfaced tonight -- a validator-clean UNH proposal was rejected at execution with 'insufficient cash' on a 100%-cash account, which needs an engineering look, not a reasoning fix. The one change for next week: before any discretionary SELL_TO_CLOSE that isn't a stop or horizon exit, I will name the specific thesis_invalidator that actually fired in the sell thesis itself -- if none of the three stated invalidators fired, the move is to hold or trim with sell_fraction, not a full discretionary close.

Weekly self-review: This week was mostly build week, not trade week - the system went from a bare skeleton to a full pipeline (data relay, validator, position sizing, watchlist triggers, insider activity, sector relative strength, post-earnings drift detection) in a handful of commits, and only opened its first two live paper positions on 7/9 (DELL) and 7/10 (HPE). Neither has closed yet, so there is no win/loss to grade - the real test of the process comes next week when these mature past a few days and I have to apply the cash-test and thesis-break discipline for real, not just in theory. What I got right: discipline held under pressure - six separate runs today all correctly said no-trade rather than forcing a mediocre setup into a rate-driven, breadth-thin tape, and both live entries were valuation-anchored (12-20x forward earnings) rather than chases into the 40-170x names topping the momentum scan. What went wrong was mostly data quality, not reasoning: the insider Form-4 feed got flagged as noisy five separate times this week because financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's Dell unwind, ALAB's post-lockup sales) bury genuine officer-conviction signals under hundreds of routine rows, a stale next_earnings field showed a past date for HPE, and the post_earnings_drift_candidate flag missed HPE's textbook drift setup because a one-time GAAP charge masked rising estimates - all bad data, not bad judgment, but they cost research time I'd rather spend on names. The one change for next week: get the insider feed pre-classified into sponsor/10b5-1 vs. discretionary officer transactions before it's handed to me, since that single fix has been the most repeated friction point of the week and is pure engineering, not agent judgment.

financial_checklists.note: Per-focus-name financial-line checklists by business model. Use the weight line: different models, different scoreboards.

TRV.label: Banks / brokers / insurers / diversified financials
TRV.weight: Rates, credit, capital, NII/NIM — not SaaS FCF heuristics.

lines.good_looks_like: NII/NIM stable or improving; deposit beta controlled.
lines.red_flag: NII collapsing with no fee offset.

lines.good_looks_like: Stable NCOs, reserves adequate, no surprise charge-offs.

lines.why: Regulatory capital constrains returns and survival.
lines.good_looks_like: CET1 / capital ratios comfortable vs requirements.
lines.red_flag: Capital shortfall risk, deposit flight narrative.

lines.why: P/B and ROE matter more than P/S.
lines.good_looks_like: Discount to history with stable ROE.

lines.why: Revisions embed rate and credit views.
lines.good_looks_like: Revisions stabilizing.

TRV.note: Answer each line briefly before a BUY. Model-specific: do not force SaaS FCF rules on capex-growth names, or ignore FCF on mature compounders.

PANW.label: Software / SaaS / platforms (subscription, high incremental margin)
PANW.weight: Growth + retention + FCF conversion + rule-of-40 style quality.

lines.why: SaaS value is durable growth and expansion.
lines.good_looks_like: Solid growth; net retention >100% if disclosed; guide intact.
lines.red_flag: Growth cliff, guide cut, or AI-at-risk seat compression.

lines.why: Mature software should convert earnings to cash.
lines.good_looks_like: Positive/rising FCF margins; gross margin stable/high.
lines.red_flag: FCF negative without hyper growth; gross margin collapse.

lines.good_looks_like: SBC as % revenue contained; buybacks offset dilution.
lines.red_flag: Huge SBC with no FCF; endless dilution.

lines.why: Growth + FCF margin is the quality screen.
lines.good_looks_like: Growth% + FCF margin% competitive for the subsector.
Revisions up or stable.
lines.red_flag: Persistent downward revisions at a rich multiple.

PANW.note: Answer each line briefly before a BUY. Model-specific: do not force SaaS FCF rules on capex-growth names, or ignore FCF on mature compounders.
